screens.title: File I/O and Standard Library Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Files are how programs persist data beyond a single run. In C, the standard library represents open files as file streams and provides a FILE pointer as the program’s handle. In this lesson you will learn how to open files in different modes, write formatted text, read lines safely, perform efficient binary reads and writes, detect file errors, and move the file position indicator for non‑sequential access. You will see concrete code examples for text output and input, a binary example that writes and reads an array of integers, and a hands-on contact manager design that uses a text file for persistence. We will emphasize safety: always check that fopen does not return NULL, always close streams with fclose, and use fgets when reading lines to avoid buffer overflow. By the end you will understand when to use fprintf versus fwrite, how to interpret fread returns, and how fseek and ftell let you jump to specific records. Keep in mind a common pitfall: binary dumps may not be portable across architectures due to endianness and padding. Ready to learn how C programs talk to the file system and reliably save and restore data?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about file streams and use the FILE pointer to open and close files safely, to write and read formatted text, and to work with binary data efficiently. You will practice checking for errors using the standard library functions, and you will understand how and when to move the file position indicator to read or rewrite specific records. Each objective is tied to a concrete skill: using fopen with the correct mode and guarding for NULL, using fprintf and fgets to produce and consume human-readable files, applying fread and fwrite to handle raw memory buffers, and using fseek and ftell to implement random access patterns. These skills matter because persistent data is central to real programs: configuration files, logs, saved user data, and binary blobs all rely on correct file handling. As you practice, you will learn a checklist to avoid common bugs: check fopen, check returns from fread/fwrite, use perror to expose system errors, and always call fclose. We also include a hands-on contact manager that exercises these objectives in a small project.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives are intentionally practical. You will open files in the correct mode and check for failure so your program doesn’t dereference NULL. You will write lines with fprintf and read them back with fgets, parsing values with sscanf or fscanf where appropriate, while avoiding unsafe use of scanf on raw input. You will write arrays to disk with fwrite and read them back with fread, verifying the number of items read. You will handle system-level failures by checking ferror and feof and calling perror to expose errno details. Finally, you will use fseek and ftell to move the file position indicator when you need random access or want to re-read a file without reopening it. Each skill will be practiced in the contact manager activity: loading contacts from a text file into a dynamic array, appending new contacts safely, and freeing memory before exit. As you practice, compare fprintf and fwrite to choose between human-readable and efficient binary representations.

screens.title: File streams and the FILE pointer
screens.narratorSegment: A file stream is an abstraction that connects your program to a file managed by the operating system. The C standard library exposes this abstraction through the FILE type; a FILE pointer is the program’s handle to an open stream. When you call fopen with a filename and a mode, the runtime opens the underlying file and returns a FILE* that you pass to functions like fprintf, fgets, fread, and fwrite. This single pointer carries state: the buffering mode, the position indicator, and error flags. A concrete example: when you open data. txt for writing, fopen returns a non‑NULL FILE*. Passing that pointer to fprintf writes formatted text into the stream’s buffer; fclose flushes buffers to disk and returns resources. A common misconception is to treat FILE objects like plain file descriptors. They are higher level: they implement buffering and formatting. Another pitfall is not checking fopen’s return; if fopen returns NULL and you call fprintf, the program may crash. Key operations to remember are checking the returned pointer, always calling fclose when done, and understanding that FILE* functions manipulate the same position indicator. Think of FILE* as the controller that all file operations use. How will you make checking fopen part of your habit?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2 › File streams
Definition

File streams and FILE pointer

A file stream is an abstract channel. fopen returns a FILE* which all file functions use. The pointer includes buffer state, the file position indicator, and error flags.

Concrete example
Open data.txt with fopen("data.txt", "w"), check for NULL, then use fprintf to write lines and fclose to flush.
Common misconception
FILE* is not a simple file descriptor. It manages buffering and formatted I/O and must be handled with library functions.
Annotated Flow
Open → Use pointer in calls → Buffering occurs → Close to flush
Check your understanding
  • What does fopen return on failure? (NULL)
  • Why call fclose? (flush buffers and release the handle)
  • What does the FILE* track besides the file name? (position and error flags)
Key Takeaway

Treat FILE* as the single source of truth for an open file; always validate and close it.

screens.title: Opening files with fopen and modes
screens.narratorSegment: Opening a file begins with the fopen call which takes a filename and a mode string. Common modes are read, write, and append: "r" requires the file to exist, "w" creates or truncates, and "a" appends. Binary forms add a trailing b, for example "rb" or "wb". There are also read/write modes that allow both reading and writing, like "r+", "w+", and "a+". Choose the mode to match your intent: use write when you want a fresh file, append to preserve existing contents, and read when you only need to inspect. Always check fopen’s return for NULL; failure can happen if the file is missing in read mode or permission is denied. A concrete scenario: when saving logs, open with "a" so existing logs are preserved; if you used "w" you would erase previous entries accidentally. Another common error is forgetting the b in binary workflows — text mode can alter newline handling on some systems. After fopen succeeds, use the FILE* until you call fclose. Habitually check the return value and report system errors with perror for clearer diagnostics. What mode will you choose when you need to add records without losing existing data?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2 › fopen and modes
Mode Reference
"r": Read mode. File must exist.
"w": Write mode. Creates or truncates.
"a": Append. Creates if needed, preserves existing data.
Binary: Add b such as "rb" or "wb" for raw bytes.
Read/Write: "r+", "w+", "a+" allow both operations with subtle differences.
Examples & Pitfalls

When saving logs use "a" to append. Using "w" would erase previous log entries. For binary snapshots, use "wb" and "rb" to avoid newline translations.

Check your code
  • Does fopen return NULL? Handle it.
  • Are you using the correct mode for binary vs text?
  • Will your choice truncate data unexpectedly?
Key Takeaway

Pick the mode to match intent and always check fopen’s return value before using the FILE pointer.

screens.title: Text file I/O: fprintf, fscanf, fgets, fputs
screens.narratorSegment: Text input and output is where most beginners start because files are human-readable and easy to inspect. Use fprintf to write formatted lines just like printf but with an explicit FILE* as the first argument. For reading, fscanf can parse formatted input but it is less safe than fgets because it does not bound line length. Prefer fgets to read a full line into a buffer with an explicit maximum size, then use sscanf or strtok to parse fields. A concrete example: open a file for writing with fopen("data. txt", "w"), check for NULL, then use fprintf(outFile, "Hello, C File input and output!\n") and fclose. For reading do fopen("data. txt", "r"), check for NULL, then call fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), inFile) and handle the trailing newline or an empty read. A common mistake is using scanf-style functions on user input without size checks; this leads to buffer overflow. Another tip is to remember that fgets keeps the newline if space permits; trim it if you need exact comparisons. Finally, check fscanf’s return value: it returns the number of items successfully read, which helps detect parsing failures. Which read function will you prefer when handling untrusted input?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2 › Text I/O
Code Walkthrough
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  FILE *outFile = fopen("data.txt", "w");
  if (outFile == NULL) {
    perror("Error opening file for writing");
    return 1;
  }
  fprintf(outFile, "Hello, C File I/O!
");
  fprintf(outFile, "The answer is %d.
", 42);
  fclose(outFile);
  return 0;
}
Reading lines safely
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  FILE *inFile = fopen("data.txt", "r");
  char buffer[256];
  if (inFile == NULL) {
    perror("Error opening file for reading");
    return 1;
  }
  if (fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), inFile) != NULL) {
    printf("Read line: %s", buffer);
  }
  fclose(inFile);
  return 0;
}
Notes
  • fgets preserves the newline if it fits; trim it for comparisons.
  • Check fscanf return value to confirm parsed items.

screens.title: Formatted vs raw: fprintf and fwrite
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between formatted text and binary writes depends on your goals. fprintf produces human-readable output with conversions and delimiters. fwrite writes raw memory from your program to the file byte-for-byte. Use fprintf for configuration, logs, and files intended to be inspected or edited by humans. Use fwrite and fread for efficient storage of large arrays, images, or when exact byte representation matters. A concrete example from the chapter writes an array of integers to numbers. bin using fwrite(numbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile). The function returns the number of items written; verify this to detect partial writes. A misconception is to assume fwrite always writes everything; on error it can write fewer items — check the returned size and use perror when appropriate. Another concern is portability: a struct's memory layout may differ across machines because of endianness and padding. If portability matters, prefer a defined textual format or a portable binary protocol. Practically, prefer fprintf for readability and fwrite for performance, and always check return values for both approaches. Which representation will you pick when data must be shared across different machines?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2 › fprintf vs fwrite
fprintf — Formatted text

Use when records should be readable and editable. Conversions like %d and %s create text output.

Example: fprintf(outFile, "Name: %s, Age: %d ", name, age);
fwrite — Raw bytes

Use for efficient block storage when exact memory representation is desired. Check returned count to ensure full write.

Example: fwrite(numbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile);
Portability note

Binary dumps of structs can break across architectures because of endianness and padding. Use text or a stable serialization for cross-platform data exchange.

screens.title: Binary I/O example: writing and reading integers
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a binary example that writes an array of integers to a file and reads it back. First we prepare an array and compute its count using sizeof. We open the file with fopen in "wb" mode for writing binary; always check fopen for NULL and call perror on failure. Calling fwrite(numbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile) writes count items; it returns the number of items actually written, so check that it matches count. After closing the file, reopen in "rb" and call fread(readNumbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile) to read the data back. Verify the returned count and then inspect the integers. This pattern is efficient because fwrite and fread transfer blocks of memory without formatting overhead. A common misconception is that fwrite preserves higher-level structure metadata; it does not. It writes raw bytes exactly as stored in memory, so endianness and padding matter. For small arrays this is simple and fast; for cross-system storage, convert values to a defined byte order or prefer text. Test the return values and handle incomplete reads or writes gracefully. How will you check that your binary transfer succeeded?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2 › Binary I/O Example
Write integers to a binary file
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main() {
  int numbers[] = {10,20,30,40,50};
  int count = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
  FILE *binFile = fopen("numbers.bin", "wb");
  if (binFile == NULL) { perror("Error opening binary file for writing"); return 1; }
  size_t written = fwrite(numbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile);
  if (written != count) { perror("Partial write"); }
  fclose(binFile);
  return 0;
}
Read the integers back
  FILE *binFile = fopen("numbers.bin", "rb");
  if (binFile == NULL) { perror("Error opening binary file for reading"); return 1; }
  int readNumbers[5];
  size_t itemsRead = fread(readNumbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile);
  if (itemsRead == count) { /* success: inspect values */ }
  else { printf("Read only %zu items
", itemsRead); }
  fclose(binFile);

screens.title: Binary safety: endianness and padding
screens.narratorSegment: Binary input and output writes exact bytes from memory, which is efficient but can be fragile across systems. Two reasons cause incompatibility: endianness and structure padding. Endianness describes byte order: some systems store multi‑byte values least significant byte first, others most significant first. If you write binary integers on one endianness and read them on another without conversion, values will be incorrect. Structure padding is how compilers align struct fields to memory boundaries, which can insert unused bytes. A struct written by one compiler on one architecture may have different padding when compiled elsewhere. A concrete scenario: writing an array of int or a struct directly with fwrite is fine for local snapshoting, but if the file must travel to another machine, prefer a defined serialization: write textual fields with fprintf or implement explicit byte-order conversion for each field before writing. A common misconception is that raw fwrite is a safe serialization for all use cases; it is not. If you must exchange binary data across systems, define a stable wire format or convert integers to network byte order before writing. In short, binary is fast but carries portability costs you must manage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2 › Binary Portability

Endianness

Byte order differs between architectures. A 32-bit integer written as bytes may be read in reverse order on another system.

Implication
Convert to a canonical byte order or use text formats to ensure portability.

Padding

Compilers may insert padding inside structs for alignment. The raw memory layout can differ between compilers and platforms.

Implication
Serialize fields explicitly rather than dumping the struct memory directly when portability is required.
Common mistake

Assuming fwrite of a struct is portable. Verify byte order and padding before relying on binary compatibility across machines.

screens.title: Error handling: ferror, feof, perror, errno
screens.narratorSegment: Robust file code checks for errors at every step. Start by testing fopen for NULL; when a system-level failure occurs, perror prints a human-friendly message that includes errno. After input and output calls, use ferror to query the stream-level error indicator to know whether operations failed, and use feof to detect end-of-file conditions when reading. A concrete sequence: fopen the file; if NULL, call perror to print the reason; after reading in a loop, check feof to differentiate end-of-file from an error; if ferror is true, call perror to get system diagnostics. For functions like fread and fwrite, inspect the returned item count; a mismatch with expected count indicates a partial operation. A common misconception is treating EOF as an error; feof returns true only when the end-of-file indicator is set, which is not an error condition by itself. Also remember that errno is set by failing system calls; calling unrelated functions before checking errno can overwrite it. When reporting errors to users, provide clear messages and fail gracefully, closing any open streams and freeing memory before exiting. How will you surface a helpful message when a file read fails?

screens.title: File seeking with fseek, ftell, and rewind
screens.narratorSegment: File seeking lets you jump to particular positions in a file instead of reading it sequentially. Use fseek to move the file position indicator: provide a stream, an offset in bytes, and an origin like SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, or SEEK_END. Call ftell to get the current offset from the file beginning; use rewind to set the pointer back to zero. These operations are valuable when working with fixed-size records or when you want to overwrite a specific record without rewriting the entire file. A concrete example writes ten characters, uses ftell to get the position, seeks to a byte offset to read a specific character with fgetc, then seeks backwards and reads again. Remember that fseek offsets are bytes, so for structured records multiply the record index by the record size. A common misconception is that seeking always succeeds; fseek can fail on streams that do not support seeking, such as some pipes. After fseek, check the return value and handle errors with perror. Also, when switching between reading and writing on the same stream, some implementations require an intervening fseek or fflush to synchronize the stream. How could you use fseek to implement a simple index for fixed-length records?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2 › Seeking & Position
Common calls
  • fseek(stream, offset, SEEK_SET|SEEK_CUR|SEEK_END)
  • ftell(stream) returns current offset
  • rewind(stream) sets offset to zero
Record access pattern
To read record n of fixed size S: fseek(stream, n * S, SEEK_SET); then fread the record.
Example snippet
FILE *f = fopen("seek_test.txt", "w+");
if (f == NULL) { perror("Error"); }
fprintf(f, "0123456789");
long pos = ftell(f); /* should be 10 */
fseek(f, 3, SEEK_SET);
int c = fgetc(f); /* '3' */
rewind(f);
int first = fgetc(f); /* '0' */
fclose(f);
Note: fseek may fail on non-seekable streams; check the return value and handle errors accordingly.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: When working with files, a few recurring mistakes account for most failures. First, failing to check fopen’s return value can lead to dereferencing NULL and crashing immediately. Second, using scanf-style functions without bounds allows buffer overflow; prefer fgets for line reads. Third, using the wrong mode, for example choosing "w" when you intended to append, can silently erase data. Fourth, ignoring return counts from fread and fwrite can hide partial input and output and data truncation. Fifth, assuming binary dumps are portable across systems leads to confusing bugs when files move between architectures. For debugging, use perror to print the system error and check errno right after a failing call. Insert fprintf to a separate log file or to stdout to trace code paths and output ftell positions to verify where reads and writes occur. If a program appears to hang on file operations, confirm you opened in the intended mode and that another process is not locking the file. A small discipline of immediate return-value checks, consistent error messages, and closing files in every error branch will make your code far more reliable. Which of these habits will you adopt first?

fullNarratorScript:
Files are how programs persist data beyond a single run. In C, the standard library represents open files as file streams and provides a FILE pointer as the program’s handle. In this lesson you will learn how to open files in different modes, write formatted text, read lines safely, perform efficient binary reads and writes, detect file errors, and move the file position indicator for non‑sequential access. You will see concrete code examples for text output and input, a binary example that writes and reads an array of integers, and a hands-on contact manager design that uses a text file for persistence. We will emphasize safety: always check that fopen does not return NULL, always close streams with fclose, and use fgets when reading lines to avoid buffer overflow. By the end you will understand when to use fprintf versus fwrite, how to interpret fread returns, and how fseek and ftell let you jump to specific records. Keep in mind a common pitfall: binary dumps may not be portable across architectures due to endianness and padding. Ready to learn how C programs talk to the file system and reliably save and restore data?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about file streams and use the FILE pointer to open and close files safely, to write and read formatted text, and to work with binary data efficiently. You will practice checking for errors using the standard library functions, and you will understand how and when to move the file position indicator to read or rewrite specific records. Each objective is tied to a concrete skill: using fopen with the correct mode and guarding for NULL, using fprintf and fgets to produce and consume human-readable files, applying fread and fwrite to handle raw memory buffers, and using fseek and ftell to implement random access patterns. These skills matter because persistent data is central to real programs: configuration files, logs, saved user data, and binary blobs all rely on correct file handling. As you practice, you will learn a checklist to avoid common bugs: check fopen, check returns from fread/fwrite, use perror to expose system errors, and always call fclose. We also include a hands-on contact manager that exercises these objectives in a small project.

These objectives are intentionally practical. You will open files in the correct mode and check for failure so your program doesn’t dereference NULL. You will write lines with fprintf and read them back with fgets, parsing values with sscanf or fscanf where appropriate, while avoiding unsafe use of scanf on raw input. You will write arrays to disk with fwrite and read them back with fread, verifying the number of items read. You will handle system-level failures by checking ferror and feof and calling perror to expose errno details. Finally, you will use fseek and ftell to move the file position indicator when you need random access or want to re-read a file without reopening it. Each skill will be practiced in the contact manager activity: loading contacts from a text file into a dynamic array, appending new contacts safely, and freeing memory before exit. As you practice, compare fprintf and fwrite to choose between human-readable and efficient binary representations.

A file stream is an abstraction that connects your program to a file managed by the operating system. The C standard library exposes this abstraction through the FILE type; a FILE pointer is the program’s handle to an open stream. When you call fopen with a filename and a mode, the runtime opens the underlying file and returns a FILE* that you pass to functions like fprintf, fgets, fread, and fwrite. This single pointer carries state: the buffering mode, the position indicator, and error flags. A concrete example: when you open data. txt for writing, fopen returns a non‑NULL FILE*. Passing that pointer to fprintf writes formatted text into the stream’s buffer; fclose flushes buffers to disk and returns resources. A common misconception is to treat FILE objects like plain file descriptors. They are higher level: they implement buffering and formatting. Another pitfall is not checking fopen’s return; if fopen returns NULL and you call fprintf, the program may crash. Key operations to remember are checking the returned pointer, always calling fclose when done, and understanding that FILE* functions manipulate the same position indicator. Think of FILE* as the controller that all file operations use. How will you make checking fopen part of your habit?

Opening a file begins with the fopen call which takes a filename and a mode string. Common modes are read, write, and append: "r" requires the file to exist, "w" creates or truncates, and "a" appends. Binary forms add a trailing b, for example "rb" or "wb". There are also read/write modes that allow both reading and writing, like "r+", "w+", and "a+". Choose the mode to match your intent: use write when you want a fresh file, append to preserve existing contents, and read when you only need to inspect. Always check fopen’s return for NULL; failure can happen if the file is missing in read mode or permission is denied. A concrete scenario: when saving logs, open with "a" so existing logs are preserved; if you used "w" you would erase previous entries accidentally. Another common error is forgetting the b in binary workflows — text mode can alter newline handling on some systems. After fopen succeeds, use the FILE* until you call fclose. Habitually check the return value and report system errors with perror for clearer diagnostics. What mode will you choose when you need to add records without losing existing data?

Text input and output is where most beginners start because files are human-readable and easy to inspect. Use fprintf to write formatted lines just like printf but with an explicit FILE* as the first argument. For reading, fscanf can parse formatted input but it is less safe than fgets because it does not bound line length. Prefer fgets to read a full line into a buffer with an explicit maximum size, then use sscanf or strtok to parse fields. A concrete example: open a file for writing with fopen("data. txt", "w"), check for NULL, then use fprintf(outFile, "Hello, C File input and output!\n") and fclose. For reading do fopen("data. txt", "r"), check for NULL, then call fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), inFile) and handle the trailing newline or an empty read. A common mistake is using scanf-style functions on user input without size checks; this leads to buffer overflow. Another tip is to remember that fgets keeps the newline if space permits; trim it if you need exact comparisons. Finally, check fscanf’s return value: it returns the number of items successfully read, which helps detect parsing failures. Which read function will you prefer when handling untrusted input?

Choosing between formatted text and binary writes depends on your goals. fprintf produces human-readable output with conversions and delimiters. fwrite writes raw memory from your program to the file byte-for-byte. Use fprintf for configuration, logs, and files intended to be inspected or edited by humans. Use fwrite and fread for efficient storage of large arrays, images, or when exact byte representation matters. A concrete example from the chapter writes an array of integers to numbers. bin using fwrite(numbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile). The function returns the number of items written; verify this to detect partial writes. A misconception is to assume fwrite always writes everything; on error it can write fewer items — check the returned size and use perror when appropriate. Another concern is portability: a struct's memory layout may differ across machines because of endianness and padding. If portability matters, prefer a defined textual format or a portable binary protocol. Practically, prefer fprintf for readability and fwrite for performance, and always check return values for both approaches. Which representation will you pick when data must be shared across different machines?

Let's walk through a binary example that writes an array of integers to a file and reads it back. First we prepare an array and compute its count using sizeof. We open the file with fopen in "wb" mode for writing binary; always check fopen for NULL and call perror on failure. Calling fwrite(numbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile) writes count items; it returns the number of items actually written, so check that it matches count. After closing the file, reopen in "rb" and call fread(readNumbers, sizeof(int), count, binFile) to read the data back. Verify the returned count and then inspect the integers. This pattern is efficient because fwrite and fread transfer blocks of memory without formatting overhead. A common misconception is that fwrite preserves higher-level structure metadata; it does not. It writes raw bytes exactly as stored in memory, so endianness and padding matter. For small arrays this is simple and fast; for cross-system storage, convert values to a defined byte order or prefer text. Test the return values and handle incomplete reads or writes gracefully. How will you check that your binary transfer succeeded?

Binary input and output writes exact bytes from memory, which is efficient but can be fragile across systems. Two reasons cause incompatibility: endianness and structure padding. Endianness describes byte order: some systems store multi‑byte values least significant byte first, others most significant first. If you write binary integers on one endianness and read them on another without conversion, values will be incorrect. Structure padding is how compilers align struct fields to memory boundaries, which can insert unused bytes. A struct written by one compiler on one architecture may have different padding when compiled elsewhere. A concrete scenario: writing an array of int or a struct directly with fwrite is fine for local snapshoting, but if the file must travel to another machine, prefer a defined serialization: write textual fields with fprintf or implement explicit byte-order conversion for each field before writing. A common misconception is that raw fwrite is a safe serialization for all use cases; it is not. If you must exchange binary data across systems, define a stable wire format or convert integers to network byte order before writing. In short, binary is fast but carries portability costs you must manage.

Robust file code checks for errors at every step. Start by testing fopen for NULL; when a system-level failure occurs, perror prints a human-friendly message that includes errno. After input and output calls, use ferror to query the stream-level error indicator to know whether operations failed, and use feof to detect end-of-file conditions when reading. A concrete sequence: fopen the file; if NULL, call perror to print the reason; after reading in a loop, check feof to differentiate end-of-file from an error; if ferror is true, call perror to get system diagnostics. For functions like fread and fwrite, inspect the returned item count; a mismatch with expected count indicates a partial operation. A common misconception is treating EOF as an error; feof returns true only when the end-of-file indicator is set, which is not an error condition by itself. Also remember that errno is set by failing system calls; calling unrelated functions before checking errno can overwrite it. When reporting errors to users, provide clear messages and fail gracefully, closing any open streams and freeing memory before exiting. How will you surface a helpful message when a file read fails?

File seeking lets you jump to particular positions in a file instead of reading it sequentially. Use fseek to move the file position indicator: provide a stream, an offset in bytes, and an origin like SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, or SEEK_END. Call ftell to get the current offset from the file beginning; use rewind to set the pointer back to zero. These operations are valuable when working with fixed-size records or when you want to overwrite a specific record without rewriting the entire file. A concrete example writes ten characters, uses ftell to get the position, seeks to a byte offset to read a specific character with fgetc, then seeks backwards and reads again. Remember that fseek offsets are bytes, so for structured records multiply the record index by the record size. A common misconception is that seeking always succeeds; fseek can fail on streams that do not support seeking, such as some pipes. After fseek, check the return value and handle errors with perror. Also, when switching between reading and writing on the same stream, some implementations require an intervening fseek or fflush to synchronize the stream. How could you use fseek to implement a simple index for fixed-length records?

The plan is to store each contact on its own line in contacts. txt as name,phone separated by a comma. When working with files, a few recurring mistakes account for most failures. First, failing to check fopen’s return value can lead to dereferencing NULL and crashing immediately. Second, using scanf-style functions without bounds allows buffer overflow; prefer fgets for line reads. Third, using the wrong mode, for example choosing "w" when you intended to append, can silently erase data. Fourth, ignoring return counts from fread and fwrite can hide partial input and output and data truncation. Fifth, assuming binary dumps are portable across systems leads to confusing bugs when files move between architectures. For debugging, use perror to print the system error and check errno right after a failing call. Let's summarize the essential ideas to carry forward. File streams provide a standard interface; fopen returns a FILE pointer that you must validate and eventually close. Text input and output functions like fprintf and fgets make files readable and editable, while binary functions like fwrite and fread are efficient for raw blocks of data. Error handling matters: check fopen for NULL, inspect fread and fwrite return counts, use ferror and feof to query stream state, and call perror to print system diagnostics derived from errno. Seeking functions such as fseek, ftell, and rewind let you implement non‑sequential access patterns such as fixed-record indexing. Keep in mind portability trade-offs: binary dumps are fast but sensitive to endianness and padding. These ideas form a practical checklist for safe file programming: check returns, prefer safe readers, validate counts, and always close streams. Keep three short rules in mind. First, validate every fopen and close files with fclose to avoid leaks and data loss. Second, prefer fgets for reading lines and check fscanf or sscanf returns when parsing formatted data; use fwrite and fread only when you understand the portability implications. Third, always check function return values and use perror with errno to provide meaningful diagnostics; for random access use fseek and ftell but check returns because not all streams are seekable. These compact habits will prevent most file input and output bugs and make your programs more reliable when persisting and restoring data.
